quests.hint: AN ISSUE SERIOUS ENOUGH TO NEED FORMAL ATTENTION, DESCRIBED IN THE REGISTER A REPORT WOULD USE
quests.explanation: MAJOR PROBLEM is the natural, formal way to describe a serious issue in professional writing. GREAT doesn't fit this sense, and LARGE or BIG describe physical size rather than seriousness, and sound too casual for a formal report.
quests.instruction: Choose the word that fits this formal context.
quests.contextSentence: The report identified staffing shortages as a ___ problem facing the hospital.

quests.hint: A RISE BIG ENOUGH TO BE WORTH MENTIONING IN A FORMAL REPORT OR STUDY
quests.explanation: SUBSTANTIAL INCREASE is the standard formal collocation for a significant rise, common in reports and academic writing. BIG, LARGE, and HIGH describe size in more casual or physical ways that don't fit this formal register.
quests.instruction: Select the word that fits this formal context.
quests.contextSentence: The study recorded a ___ increase in reading scores after the new program began.

quests.hint: HARM THAT IS SERIOUS AND EXTENSIVE, NOT JUST PHYSICALLY HEAVY OR STRONG
quests.explanation: SEVERE DAMAGE is the standard collocation for extensive harm. STRONG, HEAVY, and BIG describe physical force or size, but SEVERE specifically captures the seriousness of harm done.
quests.instruction: Find the word that naturally completes the pair.
quests.contextSentence: The hurricane caused ___ damage to homes along the coastline.

quests.hint: A BODY TEMPERATURE THAT HAS RISEN WELL ABOVE NORMAL
quests.explanation: HIGH FEVER is the only natural collocation for describing this symptom. TALL, BIG, and GREAT simply don't combine with FEVER in English, regardless of how severe it is.
quests.instruction: Find the word that naturally completes the pair.
quests.contextSentence: The child was taken to the hospital with a dangerously ___ fever.

quests.hint: THE SURFACE ABOVE YOU IN A ROOM, WHEN IT'S UNUSUALLY FAR FROM THE FLOOR
quests.explanation: HIGH CEILING is correct, even though many learners mistakenly say 'tall ceiling.' In English, TALL describes things that stand upright from the ground, like buildings or people, while HIGH describes vertical distance above a surface.
quests.instruction: Choose the word that correctly pairs with this noun.
quests.contextSentence: The old cathedral is famous for its remarkably ___ ceilings.

quests.hint: A STRUCTURE THAT RISES UPWARD FROM THE GROUND, LIKE A PERSON STANDING
quests.explanation: TALL BUILDING is correct, in contrast to a HIGH CEILING. TALL describes things that stand upright from ground level, such as buildings, trees, or people, while HIGH describes distance above a surface.
quests.instruction: Select the word that correctly pairs with this noun.
quests.contextSentence: The city's newest ___ building can be seen from almost anywhere downtown.

quests.hint: AN EVERYDAY MILD ILLNESS THAT ALMOST EVERYONE CATCHES FROM TIME TO TIME
quests.explanation: THE COMMON COLD is the fixed name for this everyday illness. FREQUENT, REGULAR, and USUAL simply don't fit this specific fixed medical expression, even though they relate to similar ideas.
quests.instruction: Find the word that naturally completes the pair.
quests.contextSentence: There's still no cure for the ___ cold, despite decades of research.

quests.hint: SOMEONE WHO TRAVELS BY PLANE VERY OFTEN, OFTEN ENROLLED IN AN AIRLINE'S REWARDS PROGRAM
quests.explanation: FREQUENT FLYER is a fixed compound term, especially in the phrase 'frequent flyer program.' COMMON, REGULAR, and USUAL don't fit this specific fixed expression, even though they're related in meaning.
quests.instruction: Choose the word that correctly completes this compound.
quests.contextSentence: As a ___ flyer, she earns enough points for a free ticket every year.

quests.hint: A SCHEDULED VISIT TO THE DOCTOR THAT HAPPENS AT SET INTERVALS, NOT JUST WHENEVER YOU'RE SICK
quests.explanation: REGULAR CHECKUP is the standard fixed medical phrase for a scheduled visit. FREQUENT, COMMON, and USUAL don't combine naturally with CHECKUP the way REGULAR does.
quests.instruction: Select the word that correctly completes this pair.
quests.contextSentence: Her doctor recommends a ___ checkup every six months.

quests.hint: AN INQUIRY THAT EXAMINES EVERY DETAIL CAREFULLY, RATHER THAN JUST BEING FINISHED OR TOTAL
quests.explanation: THOROUGH INVESTIGATION is the standard collocation emphasizing careful, detailed examination. COMPLETE, FULL, and TOTAL describe finishing something entirely, but THOROUGH specifically describes the careful method used.
quests.instruction: Find the word that naturally completes the pair.
quests.contextSentence: Auditors carried out a ___ investigation, checking every single transaction from the past year.

quests.hint: GETTING BACK EVERY CENT YOU PAID, RATHER THAN JUST PART OF IT
quests.explanation: FULL REFUND is the fixed standard business term for getting all your money back. COMPLETE, TOTAL, and WHOLE don't form this specific fixed phrase, even though they express a similar idea.
quests.instruction: Choose the word that correctly completes this pair.
quests.contextSentence: Since the product was faulty, the store offered her a ___ refund.

quests.hint: SOMEONE YOU HAVE ABSOLUTELY NO PRIOR CONNECTION TO OR KNOWLEDGE OF
quests.explanation: COMPLETE STRANGER is the standard fixed idiom for someone entirely unknown to you. FULL, ENTIRE, and WHOLE don't form this specific phrase — English speakers don't say 'a full stranger' or 'an entire stranger' — even though they express similar ideas of totality.
quests.instruction: Select the word that correctly completes this idiom.
wrongCollocations: a full stranger on the street
an entire stranger at the party
quests.contextSentence: She struck up a conversation with a ___ stranger while waiting for the train.

quests.hint: A REAL, UNFORCED CURIOSITY ABOUT SOMETHING, NOT JUST POLITE PRETENSE
quests.explanation: GENUINE INTEREST is the standard collocation for real, authentic curiosity. SINCERE, HONEST, and TRUE express similar honesty, but GENUINE is the word that naturally pairs with INTEREST in everyday English.
quests.instruction: Find the word that naturally completes the pair.
quests.contextSentence: The interviewer showed ___ interest in every answer the candidate gave.

quests.hint: AN EXPRESSION THAT COMES FROM REAL HAPPINESS, NOT ONE THAT'S FORCED OR FAKE
quests.explanation: GENUINE SMILE is the natural collocation for an authentic, unforced expression of happiness. SINCERE, HONEST, and TRUE are used for other kinds of authenticity, such as feelings or statements, but not typically for a facial expression.
quests.instruction: Choose the word that correctly completes this pair.
quests.contextSentence: Despite the long day, she gave him a warm and ___ smile.

quests.hint: WORDS OF SYMPATHY OFFERED TO SOMEONE WHO HAS RECENTLY LOST A LOVED ONE
quests.explanation: SINCERE CONDOLENCES is the standard fixed phrase used when expressing sympathy after a death. GENUINE, HONEST, and TRUE don't fit this specific formal expression, even though they relate to authenticity.
quests.instruction: Select the word that correctly completes this formal expression.
quests.contextSentence: Please accept my most ___ condolences on the loss of your grandmother.

quests.hint: MORE THAN ENOUGH WARNING TIME BEFORE SOMETHING HAPPENS, PHRASED THE WAY A FORMAL LETTER WOULD
quests.explanation: AMPLE NOTICE is the standard formal collocation for generous advance warning, common in official letters and contracts. BROAD, VAST, and IMMENSE describe size or scale, not advance warning time, so they don't fit this specific fixed business phrase.
quests.instruction: Choose the word that fits this formal register.
wrongCollocations: broad notice before the rent increase
quests.contextSentence: The landlord is required to give tenants ___ notice before any rent increase.

quests.hint: CAREFUL, RESPECTFUL THOUGHT GIVEN TO SOMETHING BEFORE MAKING AN OFFICIAL DECISION
quests.explanation: DUE CONSIDERATION is the fixed formal phrase meaning proper, careful thought. PROPER, CORRECT, and RIGHT are close in meaning but don't form this specific fixed legal and business expression.
quests.instruction: Select the word that fits this formal phrase.
quests.contextSentence: The committee promised to give the proposal ___ consideration before the next vote.

quests.hint: STARTING TO APPLY RIGHT AWAY, WITHOUT ANY DELAY, IN THE PHRASING OFFICIAL DOCUMENTS USE
quests.explanation: IMMEDIATE EFFECT is the fixed legal and official phrase for something starting right away. INSTANT, QUICK, and FAST relate to speed but don't form this specific formal expression.
quests.instruction: Find the word that naturally completes the pair.
quests.contextSentence: The new safety regulations will take ___ effect starting Monday.

quests.hint: SOMETHING HAPPENING, OFTEN USED TO DESCRIBE AN EVENT OCCURRING AT A CERTAIN TIME
quests.explanation: TAKE PLACE is a fixed idiom meaning 'to happen.' SPACE, ROOM, and SPOT all relate to physical location, but none of them completes this specific fixed expression about events occurring.
quests.instruction: Find the word that naturally completes the pair.
quests.contextSentence: The ceremony will take ___ in the garden if the weather stays clear.

quests.hint: WATCHING SOMETHING OR SOMEONE CAREFULLY OVER TIME TO MAKE SURE NOTHING GOES WRONG
quests.explanation: KEEP AN EYE ON something is a fixed idiom meaning to watch it carefully. LOOK, GLANCE, and VIEW relate to seeing, but none of them completes this specific fixed expression about ongoing watchfulness.
quests.instruction: Choose the word that correctly completes this idiom.
wrongCollocations: keep a look on the kids
keep a view on the oven
quests.contextSentence: Could you keep an ___ on the soup while I answer the door?

quests.hint: FORGETTING HOW MUCH TIME HAS PASSED BECAUSE YOU WERE SO FOCUSED ON SOMETHING ELSE
quests.explanation: LOSE TRACK OF TIME is a fixed idiom meaning to forget how much time has gone by. PATH, ROUTE, and COURSE relate to direction, but none of them completes this specific fixed expression about time awareness.
quests.instruction: Select the word that correctly completes this idiom.
quests.contextSentence: She was so absorbed in the book that she completely lost ___ of time.

quests.hint: REACHING THE END OF HOW LONG A MEETING OR EVENT WAS SCHEDULED TO LAST
quests.explanation: In this specific context, RUN OUT OF TIME is correct because the sentence is about a meeting ending early due to a scheduling limit. MONEY, PATIENCE, and ENERGY can all follow RUN OUT OF in other situations, but none fits this particular context about a room booking.
quests.instruction: Read the context carefully, then choose the word that fits this specific situation.
wrongCollocations: run out of money during a meeting
run out of patience during a booking
quests.contextSentence: The meeting had to end early because the conference room booking ran out of ___.

quests.hint: REACHING A COMPROMISE WHERE EACH SIDE GIVES UP SOMETHING, RATHER THAN ONE SIDE GETTING EVERYTHING
quests.explanation: MEET SOMEONE HALFWAY is a fixed idiom meaning to compromise. PARTWAY, MIDPOINT, and CENTER relate to distance, but none of them completes this specific fixed expression about mutual compromise.
quests.instruction: Choose the word that correctly completes this idiom.
wrongCollocations: meet at the midpoint of negotiations
meet at the center of the disagreement
quests.contextSentence: If neither side is willing to meet the other ___, the negotiation will collapse.

quests.hint: TELLING SOMEONE INFORMATION THEY WON'T WANT TO HEAR, USUALLY GENTLY AND CAREFULLY
quests.explanation: BREAK THE NEWS is a fixed idiom meaning to reveal information, often unwelcome, to someone. STORY, REPORT, and ARTICLE relate to journalism, but none of them completes this specific fixed expression about delivering information personally.
quests.instruction: Select the word that correctly completes this idiom.
wrongCollocations: break the story to the family
break the report to a friend
quests.contextSentence: Nobody wanted to be the one to break the ___ about the layoffs.

quests.hint: CANCELLING A CEREMONY THAT WAS ALREADY PLANNED, USUALLY AT THE LAST MINUTE
quests.explanation: CALL OFF THE WEDDING fits this context because the sentence specifically mentions a ceremony two days away. PARTY, DINNER, and CONCERT are all things that could be called off in other situations, but the context here points specifically to a wedding.
quests.instruction: Read the context carefully, then choose the word that fits.
quests.contextSentence: Two days before the ceremony, the couple decided to call off the ___.

quests.hint: DELAYING SOMETHING YOU NEED TO CHOOSE BETWEEN TWO OPTIONS, BECAUSE YOU CAN'T MAKE UP YOUR MIND
quests.explanation: PUT OFF THE DECISION is the natural collocation for delaying a choice. CHOICE, PLAN, and VERDICT are related in meaning, but native speakers would naturally say 'put off the decision' in this exact context, not these alternatives.
quests.instruction: Choose the word that fits this specific situation.
wrongCollocations: put off the choice for a year
quests.contextSentence: She kept putting off the difficult ___ because she couldn't decide between the two job offers.

quests.hint: STOPPING A REPEATED BEHAVIOR YOU'VE DONE FOR A LONG TIME, LIKE BITING YOUR NAILS
quests.explanation: GIVE UP THE HABIT is the natural collocation for stopping a repeated behavior. ADDICTION, ROUTINE, and PATTERN are related in meaning, but HABIT is the word that fits this specific everyday context most naturally.
quests.instruction: Select the word that fits this specific behavior.
wrongCollocations: give up the addiction of biting nails
give up the routine of biting nails
quests.contextSentence: He finally gave up the terrible ___ of biting his nails.

quests.hint: FINALLY STARTING TO PRODUCE GOOD RESULTS AFTER A LONG PERIOD OF EFFORT
quests.explanation: BEAR FRUIT is a fixed idiom meaning to finally produce good results. SEEDS, VEGETABLES, and HARVEST are all related to plants literally, but none of them completes this specific fixed metaphorical expression about success.
quests.instruction: Find the word that naturally completes the pair.
quests.contextSentence: After two years of hard work, their marketing strategy finally began to bear ___.

quests.hint: SAYING EXACTLY THE RIGHT THING THAT PERFECTLY IDENTIFIES THE REAL ISSUE
quests.explanation: HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD is a fixed idiom meaning to describe something with complete accuracy. SCREW, BOLT, and HAMMER are all related tools, but none of them completes this specific fixed idiomatic expression.
quests.instruction: Choose the word that correctly completes this idiom.
wrongCollocations: hit the screw on the head
hit the bolt on the head
quests.contextSentence: When she said the real issue was poor communication, she hit the ___ right on the head.

quests.hint: SUDDENLY REVERSING A SITUATION THAT HAD BEEN GOING BADLY
quests.explanation: TURN THE TIDE is a fixed idiom meaning to reverse a losing or negative situation. WAVE, CURRENT, and FLOW are all related to water, but none of them completes this specific fixed metaphorical expression about changing fortunes.
quests.instruction: Select the word that correctly completes this idiom.
wrongCollocations: turn the wave of the game
turn the current of the match
quests.contextSentence: The team's morale was low until one unexpected win turned the ___.
